ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Cellular immunology explains how immune cells detect and eliminate pathogens, guiding clinical decisions from diagnosis to therapy. Understanding cell types, signals, and checkpoints helps predict disease patterns and treatment responses.

sections.p: The immune system relies on specialized cells—T lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells—to recognize and destroy foreign invaders. Their interactions are orchestrated by cytokines, chemokines, and antigen presentation.

t.b: Assess lymphocyte count; low lymphocytes suggest immunodeficiency or viral infection.
Quantifies T cell subsets; low CD4 indicates HIV or other immunosuppression.
Low IgG/IgM/IgA points to antibody deficiency.

sections.p: Immune cells are not organisms but cellular effectors. Their key features include antigen specificity, memory formation, and ability to kill infected cells or neutralize pathogens.

t.b: Identifies clonal expansions in lymphoma or autoimmune disease.

sections.p: Cellular immunity is activated when antigen-presenting cells process pathogens and present peptides via MHC molecules to T cells. The cycle includes priming, clonal expansion, effector function, and memory.

t.b: Measures T cell response to specific antigens; useful in TB or vaccine assessment.

sections.p: Defects in cellular immunity lead to opportunistic infections (e.g., Pneumocystis, CMV), autoimmune disorders (e.g., type 1 diabetes), and cancers (e.g., lymphoma).

t.b: Detects latent viruses reactivated in immunosuppression.

sections.p: Diagnosis integrates clinical presentation with laboratory markers of immune function. Key tests include lymphocyte subsets, cytokine profiles, and functional assays.

t.b: Low activity suggests NK cell deficiency, predisposing to viral infections.

sections.p: Management targets the underlying immune defect and the resulting infection or malignancy. Immunomodulators, biologics, and supportive care are tailored to the specific cell pathway involved.

t.b: Provides passive antibodies in antibody deficiency; reduces infection risk.
Block inflammatory cytokines in autoimmune disease; monitor for infection.

sections.p: Remember that T cell–mediated immunity is critical for intracellular pathogens. Low CD4 counts predict opportunistic infections. Memory T cells confer long-term protection; loss indicates severe immunodeficiency.
b: Low CD4 <200 cells/µL = high risk for PCP

faq.q: What is the difference between innate and adaptive immunity?
faq.a: Innate immunity provides immediate, non‑specific defense via cells like neutrophils and NK cells. Adaptive immunity is specific, involving T and B cells that develop memory.

faq.q: Why do patients with HIV develop opportunistic infections?
faq.a: HIV destroys CD4+ helper T cells, impairing the activation of other immune cells and leading to loss of control over latent pathogens.
Yes; they dampen T cell and cytokine responses, reducing the body’s ability to fight bacteria, viruses, and fungi.
